page6_img_2.png.title: Distribution of sampled pull requests by repository size
page6_img_2.png.description: A simple two-column table listing repository size categories and the number of pull requests sampled for the study: Large — 220, Medium — 200, Small — 80. These counts sum to 500 and correspond to the stratified random sampling used in the user study (categories defined in the paper as Large: >100 developers, Medium: 25–100 developers, Small: <25 developers). The table shows the relative emphasis on larger repositories in the sampled set.

page3_img_1.png.title: CORAL architecture: socio-technical graph to reviewer recommendations
page3_img_1.png.description: A three-step pipeline diagram showing how CORAL converts software development data into reviewer suggestions. (1) “Graph Building” ingests development artifacts (icons for source control and code) and constructs a purple socio-technical graph with a central Pull Request node linked to File, Repository, WorkItem and User nodes. (2) “Graph representation learning” trains a graph convolutional model to produce distributed node embeddings (depicted as a small connected network of server-like nodes). (3) “Inductive inference” uses those embeddings to score a New PR (embedding approximated from neighbors) and output Ranked/Recommended Reviewers (silhouette icons). The figure emphasizes the flow from historical data → learned node embeddings → online recommendations for unseen pull requests.

page7_img_1.png.title: CORAL top-k accuracy and MRR for reviewer prediction
page7_img_1.png.description: A two-row table reporting accuracy and mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for CORAL’s link-prediction recommender at four cutoffs (k = 1, 3, 5, 7). Accuracy improves from 0.50 at k=1 to 0.80 at k=7, with a top-3 accuracy of 0.73; MRR likewise increases from 0.49 to 0.72 across the same k values. The results indicate that CORAL often ranks a historically invited reviewer near the top of its recommendations (the reported 0.73 top-3 accuracy matches the paper’s claim that CORAL replicates authors’ reviewer choices in 73% of PRs).

page7_img_2.png.title: User-study recommendation precision by repo size: CORAL vs rule-based model
page7_img_2.png.description: Three-row comparison of recommendation precision (fraction of recommended reviewers who would engage) for Large, Medium, and Small repositories, with columns RM (rule-based model) and CORAL. Values are: Large — RM 0.19 vs CORAL 0.37; Medium — RM 0.31ᵅ vs CORAL 0.36ᵅ; Small — RM 0.35ᵝ vs CORAL 0.23ᵝ. The superscripts (α, β) mark pairs where the difference between models is not statistically significant; only the Large-repo difference (CORAL 0.37 vs RM 0.19) was statistically significant (p = 0.013), while Medium and Small differences were not.

page6_img_1.png.title: Relations used for generating embeddings in CORAL
page6_img_1.png.description: A two-column table listing the five relation types (numbered 1–5) that CORAL uses to build the relation set R for GCN-based embedding learning. The relations are: (1) PullRequest–User — captures the author or reviewer relationship; (2) PullRequest–File — captures files modified by a pull request; (3) PullRequest–Word — captures a pull request’s semantic description via tokens; (4) File–Word — captures semantic description of a file; and (5) Word–Word — captures related words co-occurring within a window of size 5 in PR titles/descriptions. These relations are used by the model to aggregate neighbor features and encode technical and semantic interactions among users, PRs, files, and words.

page3_img_2.png.title: Socio-technical graph linking PRs, people, files, work items and token subgraph
page3_img_2.png.description: A schematic of the augmented socio-technical graph used by CORAL. The central Pull request node (annotated with properties such as title, description, target branch, created/closed dates and status) connects to File (file type, path) via a Changes edge, to Author via Creates/CommentsOn, to Reviewer via Reviews/CommentsOn, and to Work item via LinkedTo; Repository contains the pull request and work items can be ParentOf other work items. A dashed-box token subgraph (Token1..Token5) shows word tokens extracted from PR text and file names that are interlinked (co‑occurrence/PMI edges) and connected to PR and File nodes to capture semantics. The diagram emphasizes the heterogeneous, labeled relations (blue edge labels) and node attributes CORAL uses to form multi-hop paths like User–PR–Token and User–PR–File for graph convolutional learning.

page4_img_table_1.png.title: Counts of nodes and edges in CORAL's socio-technical graph
page4_img_table_1.png.description: The table lists the exact node and edge counts used to build CORAL’s socio-technical graph (data ingested from 332 repositories over the study period). Node counts: pull request 1,342,821; work item 542,866; file 2,809,805; author 18,001; reviewer 30,585; text (token) 1,104,427 — total nodes 5,858,834. Edge counts: creates 1,342,821; reviews 7,066,703; contains 1,342,821; changes 12,595,859; parentOf 148,422; linkedTo 1,252,901; commentsOn 53,506 — total edges 23,803,053. The numbers show that file and change relations dominate the graph (largest node and edge contributions), there are millions of reviewer–PR and PR–text links supporting the augmented semantic layer, and the overall scale explains the large training corpus used for the GCN-based recommendation model.

page10_img_1.png.title: Ablation results: accuracy and MRR for Words/Files configurations
page10_img_1.png.description: Table of link-prediction results from the ablation study comparing four graph configurations: (1) No words or files, (2) Words only, (3) Files only, and (4) Words + Files. Metrics reported are top-k Accuracy (k=1,3,5,7) and MRR (k=1,3,5,7). Performance is very low when neither words nor files are present (Accuracy k=1..7 = 0.02, 0.08, 0.13, 0.16; MRR k=1..7 = 0.01–0.06). Adding words alone yields modest gains (Accuracy k=1 = 0.21, k=3 = 0.30; MRR k=1 = 0.21), while files alone improve results substantially (Accuracy k=1 = 0.29, k=3 = 0.69; MRR k=1 = 0.29). The best results come from combining words and files (Accuracy k=1..7 = 0.49, 0.73, 0.77, 0.80; MRR k=1..7 = 0.49, 0.61, 0.68, 0.72), supporting the paper’s claim that file-change history and semantic (word) information together provide the largest performance boost.

page9_img_1.png.title: User study — Negative feedback categories and counts
page9_img_1.png.description: Table VII classifies negative responses from the user study into three categories with their counts and percentages: I) "This pull request is no longer relevant to me" — 71 responses (91.03%); II) "Never participate in code review" — 5 responses (6.41%); III) "Pull request does not need reviewer" — 2 responses (2.56%). These results quantify why recommended reviewers marked PRs as irrelevant and support the paper's observation that most negative feedback came from developers no longer working in the affected area or otherwise uninterested in reviewing.
